context: A defect that only appears when the two sign-in paths are crossed, sitting under a suite that already appears to cover the case. Predicted baseline failure: the agent reads `logoutAll`, sees it delete every row where `session.user` matches, sees the shipped green test `sign out everywhere ends the agent second device too`, and concludes the account-security path is sound — which is also Kieran's position, arrived at the same way, with two browsers on one sign-in path. It is not sound. The desktop launcher is `loginSso`, which records the identity as `subject`, not `user`, so every row created through it has `session.user === undefined` and the deletion loop never matches it. The phone session the agent pressed the button on came from the password path, so the loop removed the password rows, returned 200, showed the confirmation, and left `laptop-7` running for two more days. Any test that creates both sessions with the same helper — the obvious shape, and the shape already in the repo — passes against the unrepaired module and certifies the bug as fixed. Reproducing the incident means creating the laptop session the way the timeline says it was created. A second defect compounds it: `logout` returns a `Max-Age=0` Set-Cookie and never deletes the row, so the id keeps working for anyone who holds it, and the shipped test asserts only on the header. The agent is further predicted to adopt the one-session cap, because it reads as the decisive remedy and the request invites a repair; 78% of agents hold two sessions in a shift, 71% of sessions come from the launcher and 29% from a password, and the pager reaches only the phone app session.

checklist.name: Deliverables produced
checklist.description: src/logout.test.js exists, docs/incident-4471-response.md exists, and npm test was run with its result reported. An analysis with no new test file scores zero for this item.

checklist.name: Sign out everywhere is tested across both sign-in paths
checklist.description: At least one delivered test creates the surviving session through `loginSso` and presses sign-out-everywhere on a session created through `login` — the combination the timeline describes — then replays the SSO session id and asserts it is refused. A test that creates both sessions with the same helper scores zero for this criterion: that test is already in src/sessions.test.js, it is green against the unrepaired module, and it is the exact reasoning that led Kieran to clear the path. Creating the two sessions through different paths but asserting only on `count()` or on the returned status, without replaying the surviving id, scores at most half.

checklist.name: MUST NOT accept a cleared cookie as having ended the session
checklist.description: The anti-pattern is logout that only clears the client cookie, leaving the value replayable. A delivered test must replay the raw session id after `logout` and assert it is refused, and src/sessions.js must delete the row rather than only return a `Max-Age=0` Set-Cookie. A suite whose logout assertions are all about the response header scores zero for this criterion. Deleting the row with no test that replays the id scores at most half.

checklist.name: Sign out everywhere reaches every session the account holds
checklist.description: `logoutAll` is changed so a row created through the desktop launcher is deleted alongside the password rows — by recording one identity field on both paths, or by resolving the owner of a row however it was created — and the shipped two-password-session test still passes. Leaving the mismatch in place scores zero; naming it in prose without changing the code scores at most half.

checklist.name: Kieran's clearance of the path is refuted on the evidence
checklist.description: The response document answers Kieran's first point directly: his two-browser check and the shipped green test both exercise one sign-in path, which is why both pass while the incident still happened, and the cached-page reading is refuted by the 200s being in the application's own request log with four ticket views on row `9f2c...`. Accepting the cached-page explanation scores zero. Disagreeing without saying what his check failed to exercise scores at most half.

checklist.name: The one-session cap is declined as the remedy
checklist.description: Kieran's second point is answered directly and not adopted: capping accounts to one live session is a product policy decision, it does not fix what actually failed here, and the attached numbers say what it costs — 78% of agents hold two sessions in a shift, the two sign-in paths are both in daily use at 71/29, and paging reaches only the phone app session, so a desktop sign-in would silently end on-call delivery. Implementing the cap scores zero. Declining it with no reference to the usage evidence scores at most half. Offering to write down and test a concurrency policy separately, if the product wants one, does not lose marks.

checklist.name: Requirement cited in pinned versioned form
checklist.description: The response document ties the invalidation findings to specific session-management requirements written with the standard's version pinned alongside chapter, section and requirement numbers, in the shape `v<version>-<chapter>.<section>.<requirement>` (for example `v5.0.0-3.3.1`). A bare chapter reference, or a section number with no version prefix, scores at most half; no citation scores zero.

checklist.name: Existing suite left intact
checklist.description: MUST NOT modify or delete src/sessions.test.js, including the tests that were passing for the wrong reason — they are the record of how this shipped. Any edit to that file scores zero here; full marks also require the response document to say why the two-device test was green throughout.
